manuscript.title: The Importance of Inner Healing
manuscript.html:
The Importance of Inner Healing

We often talk about God healing our bodies and our physical health. We pray for sicknesses, diseases, pain, and physical restoration.

But today, I want to talk to you about the importance of letting God heal your inner self.

Because there are things we experience in life that don’t necessarily leave physical scars, but they leave wounds that can affect us for years.
manuscript.notes: Opening. Let the title sit while you introduce the distinction between physical and internal wounds.

manuscript.title: You can be delivered from the thing that hurt you and still need healing from what it taught you.
manuscript.html:
You can be delivered from the thing that hurt you and still need healing from what it taught you.

Because sometimes the wound is no longer there, but the way you learned to see through that wound remains.

You may no longer be in the situation that hurt you. You may no longer be around the people who caused you pain. You may have moved on with your life, but something inside of you has not moved on.

And that’s what I want to talk about today.

manuscript.title: OUR STARTING POINT
manuscript.html:
Psalm 147:3 (KJV) He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.

God is not only concerned with healing what is physically broken. He is concerned with healing what is broken within us.

manuscript.title: Symptoms of an Unhealed Inner Life
manuscript.html:
Symptoms of an Unhealed Inner Life

1. Resentment, a Negative View of Life, and Recurring Cycles

manuscript.title: The pain is over. The resentment remains.
manuscript.html:
Hebrews 12:15 (KJV) Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled;

Many times, we have already gone through the issue, and yet we still resent people and situations. The situation may have ended years ago, but we continue to carry the anger, frustration, and resentment that came from it. We have physically moved past it, but emotionally we are still there.

manuscript.title: When old pain shapes the present
manuscript.html:
Proverbs 28:1 (KJV) The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.

Things can be perfectly okay in our lives, and yet we have such a negative view of life. We expect things to go wrong. We expect people to disappoint us. We have a difficult time enjoying what is good because we’re constantly anticipating something bad. Sometimes life isn’t as negative as we think it is. Sometimes we’re seeing life through the lens of what happened to us.

manuscript.title: When old pain shapes the present
manuscript.html:
Proverbs 15:15 (KJV) All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.

We get stuck in the same cycles of life, whether it’s the same patterns, the same circles, or even the same kinds of relationships. We find ourselves repeating the very things that have hurt us. Sometimes we change our environment without ever addressing what is happening inside of us.

And the problem is that until we address what is happening within us, we can continue repeating the same patterns in completely different circumstances.

manuscript.title: Recurring Thoughts, Sin, and Ultimately Unbreakable Addictions
manuscript.html:
2. Recurring Thoughts, Sin, and Ultimately Unbreakable Addictions

John 8:34 (KJV) Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.

manuscript.title: What we replay
manuscript.html:
One telltale sign that we have not healed is our inability to break free from the overwhelming amount of recurring thoughts. We constantly revisit conversations, situations, memories, and things that have happened to us. We replay them in our minds, sometimes imagining what we should have said or what we could have done differently. The situation is over, but our minds continue living in it.

2 Corinthians 10:5 (KJV) Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;

Romans 6:16 (KJV) Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?

manuscript.title: What we turn to
manuscript.html: Another sign is the inability to break away from sins that give us comfort. Look at your life right now. What do you do when you feel stressed? Where do you run when life gets difficult? Sometimes we develop habitual sins because they temporarily make us feel better. Instead of dealing with what is hurting us, we look for something to distract us from the pain.

manuscript.title: What begins to control us
manuscript.html:
A sign that we have not been healed is our inability to get out of addictions that are damaging us. We know what we’re doing is bad for us. We recognize the consequences. We say, “Just one more time,” or, “This will be the last time.” And yet we keep returning to the same thing.

1 Corinthians 6:12 (KJV) All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.

Sometimes the behavior isn’t just about wanting to do something wrong. Sometimes we’re using the behavior to find relief from something we have never properly dealt with.

That does not excuse sin, but it helps us understand why some things become so difficult to break.

We have to deal with the behavior, but we also have to address what keeps driving us back to it.

manuscript.title: SECTION TWO · LOOK WITHIN
manuscript.html:
How to Identify the Wounds

Psalm 139:23–24 (KJV) Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.

In order to be free from these things, we must first identify what is causing the pain.

We have to be willing to look inward and ask ourselves some difficult questions. Some people are truly suffering. When a person tells me that they’re going through depression, or that they cannot seem to break free from a sin, I believe them. I believe that what they’re experiencing is real. Sometimes people are fighting battles internally that we know absolutely nothing about.

manuscript.title: We have learned to function with the pain instead of actually dealing with it.
manuscript.html:
Proverbs 14:10 (KJV) The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.

Sometimes it’s a lack of faith, but many times it’s a lack of healing. We are quick to tell people to have more faith, to pray more, or to just get over it. And while faith and prayer are important, sometimes we fail to recognize that a person is genuinely hurting. Not every struggle with depression or unwanted thoughts is a spiritual failure.

Many times, it’s because you have not allowed God to cover your wounds with His healing grace. You have allowed God to change certain things about your life, but there are still places in your heart that you have not allowed Him to touch.

And sometimes that’s because we don’t even recognize how deeply something has affected us.

We have learned to function with the pain instead of actually dealing with it.

manuscript.title: THE POWER OF UNHEALED HURT
manuscript.html:
The Ability of Pain and Hurt to Control Us

Proverbs 18:14 (KJV) The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?

When we let God heal us, we begin to put an end to the thoughts and habits that have burdened us, because they no longer have the same hold over our lives.

The burden begins to lose its power when the wound that has been feeding it begins to heal.

Think about what happens when you’re physically injured. Even if you’re capable of continuing with your day, the pain changes how you move, how you react, and sometimes even how you treat other people.

The same thing happens internally.

Proverbs 15:13 (KJV) A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.

manuscript.title: What hurt does to us
manuscript.html: When you’re hurt, it makes it very difficult to function. You can be physically present somewhere while emotionally being completely somewhere else. Things that should be simple become exhausting because you’re carrying something internally.

manuscript.title: What hurt does to us
manuscript.html: When you’re hurt, it makes you biased. You begin judging people and situations through the experience of what happened to you. Someone can have completely innocent intentions, but because of what you’ve experienced before, you assume the worst.

manuscript.title: What hurt does to us
manuscript.html: When you’re hurt, it muddies the waters. Your judgment becomes clouded. You have a difficult time separating what is actually happening from what you are feeling. Sometimes you aren’t responding to the present situation. You’re responding to a previous wound that the present situation reminded you of.

manuscript.title: A VISUAL MODEL
manuscript.html:
Hurt Will Make You:

Proverbs 19:11 (KJV) The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
manuscript.notes: Point to each node. This visual summarizes the prior three observations; it is not a clinical diagnosis.

manuscript.title: Hurt will make you…
manuscript.html: Hold on to things longer than necessary. You continue carrying conversations, offenses, and situations that should have been left behind a long time ago. Sometimes the other person has moved on, but you’re still emotionally attached to what happened.

manuscript.title: Hurt will make you…
manuscript.html: Exaggerate situations. Something small happens, but because it touches an old wound, your response becomes much greater than the situation itself. It isn’t necessarily just about what happened today. It’s about everything that happened before.

manuscript.title: Hurt will make you…
manuscript.html: Cut people off who are completely unrelated to your current situation. You begin treating people as though they are responsible for things they never did. You punish people in your present because of what someone else did in your past.

manuscript.title: Hurt will make you…
manuscript.html:
Remain unaccountable for your behavior and shift the blame to everyone and everything else. Because you’ve been hurt, you begin justifying your reactions. And instead of recognizing when you’re wrong, you blame your circumstances, your past, and the people around you.

And we have to understand that while the pain we experienced may not have been our fault, that does not mean we are no longer responsible for how we treat other people.

Galatians 6:5 (KJV) For every man shall bear his own burden.

We cannot allow what someone did to us to become the reason we continue hurting ourselves and others.

manuscript.title: SECTION THREE · IDENTIFYING HURT
manuscript.html:
Identifying Hurt

Jeremiah 6:14 (KJV) They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.

I find this scripture interesting because God was addressing people who were treating a serious problem as though it were something small.

They were declaring peace when there was no peace.

And sometimes we do the same thing internally. We convince ourselves that we’re okay. We say we’ve moved on, that nothing is wrong, and that everything is fine.

But just because we have learned to live with something doesn’t mean that it has been healed.

So how do we identify what is actually hurting us?

Proverbs 20:5 (KJV) Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out.

manuscript.title: How do we identify the wound?
manuscript.html:
1. Who Hurt You?

Put a name on it.

Who was actually responsible for the pain you experienced?
manuscript.notes: Preview all five, then walk each question one at a time.

manuscript.title: Who hurt you?
manuscript.html:
Was it a parent? A friend? A spouse? A leader? Someone you trusted?

Sometimes we are unwilling to acknowledge who actually hurt us, and because of that, we begin projecting that pain onto everyone else.

When you identify who actually hurt you, you’ll stop blaming people who are not responsible for your current pain.

You’ll begin to recognize that not everyone is the person who hurt you.

manuscript.title: What did they do?
manuscript.html:
2. What Did They Do?

What actually happened to you?

Not just how you felt about it, but what actually took place?

What was said? What was done? What happened?

Proverbs 18:13 (KJV) He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.

Sometimes we need to be able to separate the facts of what happened from the emotions that came afterward.

Because when we don’t understand what actually hurt us, we begin treating every similar situation as a trigger.

But when you recognize what actually happened, you’ll stop treating every situation as though it is the same situation that hurt you.

Not every disagreement is rejection. Not every correction is an attack. Not every difficult conversation is someone trying to hurt you.

manuscript.title: How were you hurt?
manuscript.html:
3. How Were You Hurt?

Were you hurt physically, emotionally, or mentally?

Was it something someone did to you? Something someone said? Was it a betrayal, abandonment, rejection, or disappointment?

Proverbs 18:19 (KJV) A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle.

It’s important to understand how we were hurt because not every wound is the same.

And when we fail to distinguish between different kinds of pain, we begin treating every offense as though it deserves the same response.

But when you understand how you were hurt, you’ll stop giving every offense the same amount of importance and weight.

You will begin learning to respond to situations according to what they actually are, rather than according to how much they remind you of something else.

manuscript.title: Why were you hurt?
manuscript.html:
4. Why Were You Hurt?

What was the actual reason you were hurt?

This is an important question because sometimes we spend years blaming ourselves for things that were never our fault.

We ask ourselves, “What did I do wrong? Why wasn’t I good enough? Why did they treat me that way?”

But sometimes the answer is much simpler than we want to believe.

People can be cruel. People can be selfish. People can be evil.

Not everything someone does to you is a reflection of something wrong with you.

Sometimes people make terrible decisions, and you suffer the consequences of those decisions.

When you begin recognizing that, you’ll stop making yourself the reason for all your problems.

You’ll understand that what someone did to you doesn’t have to define who you are.

manuscript.title: When were you hurt?
manuscript.html:
5. When Were You Hurt?

This one can be difficult.

Because many times we were hurt as children or young adults, and we’ve buried those experiences so deeply that we’ve almost forgotten about them.

But although we may have forgotten about the situation, the effects of that situation can still influence our lives.

Sometimes we develop ways of thinking and behaving when we’re young because of what we experienced, and we carry those same patterns into adulthood.

We learned to protect ourselves, to avoid people, to expect rejection, or to keep our emotions hidden.

Psalm 27:10 (KJV) When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.

And now, years later, those same patterns continue affecting our relationships, our decisions, and the way we see ourselves.

Something that happened twenty years ago can still be influencing how you respond to something that happened yesterday.

But when you begin recognizing when the wound was formed, you’ll stop bringing your past into your present.

You begin realizing that you are not the same person you were when that happened.

You are no longer in that situation.

And the people who are in your life today should not have to pay for what happened to you years ago.

manuscript.title: SECTION FOUR · THE ROAD TO HEALING
manuscript.html:
How Do We Heal?

Proverbs 17:22 (KJV) A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.

Proverbs 4:23 (KJV) Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.

Now, I want to pause here because the answer to this question is almost always the same.

Forgiveness.

It seems like every message we preach about healing eventually ends with forgiveness.

And forgiveness is absolutely necessary.

But today, I want to take this a little further than forgiveness.

Because I think sometimes we teach people to forgive without ever teaching them what it actually means to heal.

manuscript.title: Choosing not to retaliate
manuscript.html:
David and Saul: Choosing Not to Retaliate

1 Samuel 24:12 (KJV) The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee.

Look at the relationship between David and Saul.

Saul had turned against David. He pursued him, wanted to kill him, and made his life incredibly difficult.

David had every reason to resent Saul.

And yet, when David had an opportunity to kill Saul, he refused.

He had the ability to retaliate. He could have taken matters into his own hands and justified it by pointing to everything Saul had done to him.

But he didn’t.

Romans 12:19 (KJV) Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.

David was able to maintain his composure even while dealing with someone who had treated him unjustly.

He decided that Saul’s actions were not going to determine his own actions.

He would not allow the way Saul treated him to determine the kind of man he would become.

manuscript.title: David spared Saul. David still kept his distance.
manuscript.html:
But notice something else.

1 Samuel 24:22 (KJV) And David sware unto Saul. And Saul went home; but David and his men gat them up unto the hold.

David spared Saul, but he didn’t immediately go back to living under Saul’s authority as though nothing had happened.

He continued maintaining distance.

And I think that’s important because sometimes we confuse forgiveness with the immediate restoration of a relationship.

David could choose not to retaliate while still recognizing the danger of the situation.

Which brings me to these questions:

What is forgiveness? How do we actually know we have healed? And how do we forgive when it’s difficult?

manuscript.title: TWO DIFFERENT WORKS
manuscript.html:
Forgiveness Does Not Equal Healing

Ephesians 4:31–32 (KJV) Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.

Forgiveness does not equal healing. Forgiveness is necessary, but forgiveness and healing are not exactly the same thing. Forgiveness deals with what we are choosing to release. Healing deals with what has happened within us.

Many times we think, “Well, I forgave this person, so I must be okay now.” And then we’re surprised when we still feel pain, when certain memories still bother us, or when certain situations still affect us. We begin questioning whether we’ve actually forgiven them.
manuscript.notes: Keep both terms visible as you explain the difference.

manuscript.title: Releasing the debt doesn't instantly repair the damage.
manuscript.html:
But we make a mistake anytime we confuse letting go of the debt with actually feeling compensated or whole. Forgiveness means that I am choosing not to continue holding this debt against you. But that doesn’t automatically mean that everything you damaged has been restored.

Healing is separate from forgiveness. I can forgive you and still not forget what you did. The memory of what happened can remain even after I’ve made the decision to forgive.

Colossians 3:13 (KJV) Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.

manuscript.title: I can forgive you for breaking my leg.
manuscript.html: Your actions can still cause me pain. Think about it this way: If you accidentally break my leg, I can forgive you for breaking my leg. I can genuinely forgive you. I don’t have to be angry with you, and I don’t have to hold it against you.

manuscript.title: But my leg is still broken.
manuscript.html:
But guess what? My leg is still broken. The pain is still there. I forgave you, but the injury continues to hurt until it heals. Forgiveness didn’t automatically restore the bone. Healing is still necessary.

Healing starts with forgiveness, but that’s not how the entire process is resolved. There is more that has to happen. There is something within us that needs to be restored.

And I think sometimes that’s where we struggle.

We’ve made the decision to forgive, but we haven’t allowed ourselves to go through the process of healing.

We’re frustrated because we think we should be over it by now.

But just because you’ve forgiven someone doesn’t mean that the pain they caused has immediately disappeared.

manuscript.title: Healing Can Be Progressive
manuscript.html:
Healing Can Be Progressive

Mark 8:22–25 (KJV)

In this passage, Jesus encounters a blind man in Bethsaida.

The people bring this man to Jesus and ask Him to touch him.

Jesus takes the man by the hand, leads him out of the town, and begins healing him.

But something very interesting happens.

After Jesus first touches the man, He asks him whether he can see anything.

The man responds in verse 24:

manuscript.title: THE FIRST TOUCH
manuscript.html:
Mark 8:24 (KJV) And he looked up, and said, I see men as trees, walking.

The man could see, but he couldn’t see clearly.

Then the Bible tells us in verse 25:

manuscript.title: THE SECOND TOUCH
manuscript.html:
Mark 8:25 (KJV) After that he put his hands again upon his eyes, and made him look up: and he was restored, and saw every man clearly.

Jesus touched him again, and his sight was completely restored.

manuscript.title: PROGRESSIVE RESTORATION
manuscript.html:
Now, I’m not saying that God has to heal everyone in stages.

But what I find interesting about this miracle is that we see a man who experienced healing before he experienced complete clarity.

He was no longer in the same condition he was in before Jesus touched him, but there was still more restoration to take place.

And sometimes that’s what healing looks like in our own lives.

We have made progress. We’re not where we used to be. Certain things no longer affect us the same way.

But there may still be areas where we need greater healing and clarity.

Philippians 1:6 (KJV) Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:

We need to allow God to continue His work in us.

manuscript.title: Healing sets new boundaries
manuscript.html:
Healing Sets New Boundaries

Proverbs 22:3 (KJV) A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.

As we heal, we begin understanding what is healthy and what is not.

We recognize that we can forgive someone without continuing to place ourselves in situations where we are repeatedly hurt.

We learn that having boundaries does not mean that we are bitter.

Sometimes it means we have developed wisdom.

We can love people without allowing them unlimited access to our lives.

We can forgive people without pretending that their actions have no consequences.

manuscript.title: Healing defines relationships
manuscript.html:
Healing Defines Relationships

Romans 12:18 (KJV) If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.

Healing helps us understand our relationships more clearly.

We begin to recognize which relationships are healthy, which ones need to change, and which ones require distance.

We stop expecting every person to make up for what someone else failed to give us.

We stop placing expectations on people that have nothing to do with them.

And we begin learning how to love people without constantly operating out of fear, resentment, or insecurity.

manuscript.title: Healing renews clarity
manuscript.html:
Healing Renews or Replenishes Clarity

Ephesians 4:23 (KJV) And be renewed in the spirit of your mind;

This is something I think is very important.

Remember what we said earlier about hurt muddying the waters?

When we’re hurting, our ability to see situations clearly can become affected.

But healing begins restoring that clarity.

Things that once triggered us don’t necessarily have the same effect.

Situations that once overwhelmed us become easier to navigate.

We begin seeing people for who they actually are instead of constantly seeing them through the experiences of our past.

manuscript.title: You remember what happened. You no longer have to keep living in it.
manuscript.html:
Healing doesn’t necessarily erase what happened to you. It changes the way what happened to you continues to affect you.

And sometimes one of the greatest signs that you’ve healed is that something which once had tremendous control over your emotions no longer controls how you live.

You remember what happened, but you no longer have to keep living in it.

manuscript.title: How do we actually heal?
manuscript.html:
How Do We Heal?

So how do we actually begin experiencing this healing?

1. Through the Power of God
manuscript.notes: This is the practical three-part response. Advance through each element separately.

manuscript.title: HOW WE HEAL · 1/3
manuscript.html:
Psalm 147:3 (KJV) He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.

Ultimately, our healing comes from God.

There are things we can work through, things we can understand, and things we can learn about ourselves.

But there is a work that God can do within us that we cannot accomplish through our own strength alone.

We need to allow Him into the places that we’ve been afraid to confront.

We need to let Him deal with the bitterness, resentment, pain, and experiences we’ve carried for so long.

Sometimes we’re asking God to change our circumstances when what we really need is for Him to heal something within us.

manuscript.title: Through genuine processing and conversation
manuscript.html:
2. Through Genuine Processing of Our Emotions and Feelings, Through Conversations

James 5:16 (KJV) Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.

Sometimes we need to talk about what happened.

We need to process what we’re feeling instead of constantly suppressing it.

We need to have honest conversations with people we trust, with people who can pray with us, encourage us, and help us work through what we’re experiencing.

Proverbs 11:14 (KJV) Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

Sometimes that may include receiving wise counsel or professional support.

Not everything is resolved by pretending that we are fine.

Sometimes we have buried things so deeply that we’ve convinced ourselves they no longer affect us.

But healing involves being willing to confront those emotions honestly.

Being able to acknowledge that something hurt you does not make you weak.

Being able to talk about what happened does not mean you have failed spiritually.

And sometimes those conversations are part of how we begin understanding what actually needs to be healed.

manuscript.title: Through recognizing and admitting the wound
manuscript.html:
3. Through Actually Recognizing and Admitting That There Is Something Wrong

Psalm 139:23 (KJV) Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:

One of the greatest obstacles to healing is refusing to acknowledge that we are hurt.

Sometimes we’re so accustomed to living a certain way that we don’t even recognize something is wrong.

We think our reactions are normal. We justify our behavior. We blame everyone around us.

But we never stop to ask ourselves, “Why am I reacting this way? Why does this bother me so much? Why do I keep returning to the same things?”

There comes a point where we have to be honest with ourselves and with God.

Psalm 51:6 (KJV) Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.

We have to admit that there are things inside of us that need attention.

We have to stop pretending that because we are functioning, we must be healed.

And we have to be willing to say, “God, there is something here that I have not dealt with. There is something here that still hurts. There is something in me that needs to change.”

Because we cannot continue ignoring our wounds and expect them to stop affecting our lives.

We have to be willing to let God heal us.

manuscript.title: INVITATION · COME TO THE HEALER
manuscript.html:
Invitation: Come to the Healer This Morning

Isaiah 61:1 (KJV) The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;

This morning, I want to invite you to come to the healer.

Not just with your physical sicknesses. Not just with the things that people can see.

But with the things you’ve been carrying internally.

The hurt that you’ve learned to hide. The resentment that you haven’t been able to let go of. The memories that still bother you. The habits that you continue returning to. The things that happened years ago that still affect how you live today.

manuscript.title: Bring Him the places you have learned to hide.
manuscript.html:
Maybe you’ve forgiven the person who hurt you, but you’ve never actually dealt with the pain they caused.

Maybe you’ve been delivered from the situation, but you’re still living with what that situation taught you.

Maybe you’ve spent years convincing yourself that you’re okay, but deep down you know there are still things that need to be healed.

I want you to understand that God is concerned about those things too.

He is concerned about your heart, your thoughts, your emotions, and the things you’ve experienced.

And you don’t have to continue carrying those wounds without bringing them before Him.

manuscript.title: THE INVITATION
manuscript.html: Matthew 11:28 (KJV) Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

manuscript.title: You can be delivered from what hurt you and still need healing from what it taught you.
manuscript.html:
You can be delivered from what hurt you and still need healing from what it taught you.

So this morning, don’t just ask God to change what is happening around you.

Ask Him to heal what is happening within you.

Come to the healer this morning.
